name: SFU Students Explore Tanzanian Climate Solutions

content.text: The programme showcased the innovative use of drone technology to assess vital soil nutrients across AKU-ACER's living laboratory, which includes coffee, flower, and avocado plantations. This initiative fostered a vibrant exchange of knowledge, culture, and technical expertise.

"When I reflect on the trip, I have immense gratitude for the cultural exchange," said Azzam Haq, a student at SFU. "One day we're on a safari, and the next day we're jumping with the Maasai... And then the next day, we're out in the fields in the avocado trees, flying our drones. So, I just think it's kind of beautiful how we were able to do so much in so little time and meet so many people, across three different universities... immense gratitude."

Professor Woo Soo Kim, expressed his satisfaction with the field school saying, "Our second mechatronics engineering field trip was completed and it's successful. During these two weeks... we had two workshops and then the student's demonstration and a very tight interaction with the local farmers and local researchers and friends."

He stressed the significance of seeing climate issues firsthand, adding, "It's not just about the knowledge, but... how we can try different technologies from the mechatronic engineering to tackle those issues and challenges."

SFU PhD student Pranjal Biswas noted key contrasts in farming practices, observing, "The cultural approach to agriculture in Tanzania has a huge emphasis on involving the community... This differs a lot from Western agriculture practices... Coming here was really important to see how the technology... might end up being used differently in Tanzania."

"I remember standing in the field watching a farmer explain how difficult it is to know what their soil really needs... It made me realize how deeply personal agriculture is," said Timothy John Suarez, an SFU student. "It's not just about crops or data, it's about people's livelihoods... This experience has changed how I see my role not just as someone who's building solutions, but as someone who's building with and for others."

NM-AIST PhD student Liston Kiwoli praised AKU-ACER's facilities, saying, "I've learnt that for successful research, we need either an environment where we can collect samples or... get data and then go back to the laboratory and analyze them to get results."

Ramadhani Sinde, NM-AIST Senior Lecturer, emphasized future collaboration, remarking, "It was great experience... we exchanged a lot... I see there is room of collaboration... I'm hoping to continue with this collaboration."

SFU MSc student Hasti Mohammadi reflected, "Seeing parts of the world you never thought you'd see makes you realize how pointless some of your worries are-and how the world is so much bigger than you."

Professor Emmanuel Sulle, Director at AKU-ACER underlined the partnership's importance, highlighting its role in enabling young engineers to "connect technical work with social and cultural contexts, and integrate science with its real-world users."

The 2025 CAPESTONE Field School stands as evidence of how international collaboration can drive innovation, foster cultural understanding, and deepen appreciation for the real-world impact of a living laboratory.

content.title: SFU Students Explore Tanzanian Climate Solutions
content.author: carol.oyola
content.description: Nine students from Simon Fraser University's (SFU) Mechatronics Systems Engineering Laboratory visited AKU's Arusha Climate and Environmental Research Centre (AKU-ACER) for the CAPESTONE field school. Led by Professor Woo Soo Kim, they underwent a two-week immersive experience from April 28 to May 9, 2025 at the site. A postdoctoral fellow and five researchers from the Nelson Mandela African Institution of Science and Technology (NM-AIST) joined them as well.
